title.text:
Seeing: pixels,
features and neurons

objects.text: How can a machine read a picture when all it has is numbers?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 1 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. In Session 0 you saw the big picture: the types of AI, the training loop, gradient descent and backpropagation. Today we open the box. We start with the simplest question: how can a machine read a picture when all it has is numbers?

By the end you will have scored a neuron by hand and watched a small network learn to read handwriting, with real numbers from a real run.

objects.text: By the end of today you will have

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.70.png

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.70.png

slides.notes:
Here is what you leave with. You can explain how a picture becomes numbers, in grey and in colour. You can score a neuron by hand, and say what its weights mean. And you can read the result of a small network that reads handwritten digits, including where it fails.

The same thinking applies to a scanned invoice, an identity photo or a photo of stock in a depot. Nothing to submit, nothing to be tested on.

title.text:
Your two hours: the ideas, a live
demonstration, and a paper exercise

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_e986ab49.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: No computer is needed from you. I run the demonstration and you watch, ask and join in.

slides.notes:
Today has three big parts. First the ideas, about thirty-five minutes: how a picture becomes numbers, what a neuron is, and how layers of neurons read a picture. Then a demonstration, about twenty-five minutes, where I train a small network on handwritten digits and you watch it learn.

After the break you score a neuron by hand on paper for twenty-five minutes. Then fifteen minutes on what this means for your own work.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: One square of a picture, stored as a number (grey) or three numbers (colour).
A measurement taken from the input, such as the amount of ink in the middle.
A weighted checklist: it multiplies, adds and compares to give one answer.
How much one question counts in a neuron. Training adjusts the weights.
A row of neurons that look at the same inputs. A network stacks layers.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_grid_0.70.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.70.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_robot_0.70.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_switch_0.70.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_doc_0.70.png

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Pixel. One square of a picture, stored as a number (grey) or three numbers (colour).

Feature. A measurement taken from the input, such as the amount of ink in the middle.

Neuron. A weighted checklist: it multiplies, adds and compares to give one answer.

Weight. How much one question counts in a neuron. Training adjusts the weights.

Layer. A row of neurons that look at the same inputs. A network stacks layers.

title.text:
A picture is a grid of numbers,
one number for each square

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t01_pixels_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A picture is a grid of numbers, one number for each square

objects.text: The computer never sees a 3. It sees 64 numbers.

runs.text: Each square is a pixel.
Here 0 is white and 16 is the darkest ink.
Think of a mosaic floor: every tile has one shade.

slides.notes:
Start with the picture. On the right is a handwritten 3. On the left is what the computer actually receives. The picture is an 8 by 8 grid, so 8 times 8 is 64 squares, and each square is one number from 0, white, to 16, darkest ink.

Think of a mosaic floor in a hotel lobby: every tile has one shade, and from far away you see a pattern. A square of the picture is called a pixel. This is a real image from the digits set that comes with scikit-learn, a free data science library.

title.text:
A colour pixel is three numbers:
how much red, green and blue

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t01_rgb_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A colour pixel is three numbers: how much red, green and blue

objects.text: Mix three lights and you can make any colour on a screen.

runs.text: 8 x 8 x 3 = 192 numbers for this tiny picture.
A 1,000 by 1,000 photo has 3,000,000 numbers.

slides.notes:
Colour needs more numbers. Imagine three torches shining on a wall, one red, one green, one blue, each with a dial from 0 to 255. Turn all three high and you get white. Mix red and green and you get yellow. So every pixel is three numbers, called RGB.

This tiny sunrise has 8 times 8 pixels times 3 numbers, which is 192 numbers. I drew it with a short script, so it is my own picture. A photo from your phone has millions of pixels. To keep it simple I leave out how files are compressed.

title.text: A feature is a measurement taken from the picture

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t01_features_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A feature is a measurement taken from the picture

objects.text: One measurement on a handwritten 0 and 1 already separates most of them.

runs.text: Feature 1: how much ink in total.
Feature 2: ink in the centre strip. A 0 has a hole there.
A person drew the red line: right 352 times in 360.

slides.notes:
Raw numbers are too many to reason about, so we take measurements. A loan officer does the same: they do not read your whole life story, they look at income, years in the job and past arrears. Those are features. Here I took two features from each handwritten 0 and 1: total ink, and the ink in the centre strip, where a 0 has a hole and a 1 has a stroke.

One horizontal line on the second feature is right for 352 of 360 digits. The numbers are from the 360 zeros and ones in the scikit-learn digits.

title.text:
A neuron is a weighted checklist:
tick, multiply, add, compare

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t01_checklist_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A neuron is a weighted checklist: tick, multiply, add, compare

objects.text: A payment-risk checklist with three questions is a neuron.

runs.text: A tick is 1 and a blank is 0.
The weight says how much the question matters.
Add the points. At 4 or more, a person checks.

slides.notes:
Here is the idea behind everything today. A payments clerk checks three things. Is the amount over UGX 1,200,000?

That counts 3 points. Is the payee new?

That counts 2. Is it outside office hours?

That counts 1. For this payment the first two are ticked, so 1 times 3, plus 1 times 2, plus 0 times 1, makes 5. The rule says 4 or more goes to a person. That is a neuron: multiply each answer by its weight, add, and compare with a cut-off.

Real neurons use a smoother cut-off, but the idea is the same.

title.text:
The same checklist gives three
different answers on three payments

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_coin_0.50.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_clock_0.50.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shop_0.50.png

objects.text: C is a large payment that passes. The weights decide, and someone chose them.

slides.notes:
Let us score three payments by hand. A is the one we saw: 3 plus 2 plus 0 is 5, so a person checks it. B is small, to a new payee, at night: 0 plus 2 plus 1 is 3, so it goes through. C is large, but to a supplier you know, in office hours: 3 plus 0 plus 0 is 3, so it also goes through.

Would you accept that?

Someone chose these weights. A different finance manager might weigh the amount more heavily. In a trained network, the weights are not chosen by a person. Training finds them, and that is the next idea.

title.text:
A network stacks layers: 64 numbers
in, 16 neurons, 10 scores out

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t01_layers_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A network stacks layers: 64 numbers in, 16 neurons, 10 scores out

objects.text: Think of 16 clerks who each look for one thing, then 10 managers who each decide on one digit.

runs.text: Each neuron has 64 weights, one per pixel.
Those 1,210 numbers are the parameters.

slides.notes:
Now stack neurons. Our digit network takes the 64 pixel numbers. Sixteen neurons in the middle each have their own checklist of 64 weights. Ten neurons at the end each give one score, one for each digit 0 to 9. Count the settings: 64 times 16 weights is 1,024, plus 16 cut-offs, plus 16 times 10 weights is 160, plus 10 more cut-offs.

That is 1,210 numbers, and they are the parameters you met in Session 0. A large language model has billions, but the idea is the same.

title.text:
After training, each neuron has a
favourite: one fires almost only for 0s

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t01_weights_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: After training, each neuron has a favourite: one fires almost only for 0s

objects.text: Look at what each neuron fires for.

runs.text: Neuron 13: its 30 strongest images were all 0s.
Neuron 8: 27 of its 30 were 9s.
The weight pictures look messy. The behaviour is clearer.

slides.notes:
Here are the weights of eight of the sixteen neurons, drawn as pictures: dark where ink adds to the score, red where it subtracts. They look messy. So I also asked a different question: which training images make each neuron fire hardest?

Neuron 13 fired hardest for 30 images and all 30 were zeros. Neuron 8 liked nines. Nobody told the network to look for a loop or a stroke. It found whatever lowered the error. Not every neuron is this neat, and that is why people say networks are hard to explain. This is a real run, recorded on 5 November 2026.

title.text:
One image goes in, 16 neurons
react, and the 3 wins with 96%

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t01_forward_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: One image goes in, 16 neurons react, and the 3 wins with 96%

objects.text: Gold bars are the neurons that fired strongly for this 3.

runs.text: Layer one reacts to the pixels.
Layer two turns those reactions into 10 scores.
The scores add to 100%: the biggest is the answer.

slides.notes:
Now follow one image through. The 3 goes in. Each of the sixteen middle neurons does its weighted checklist, and the tall bars show how strongly each one fired. A neuron with a negative total simply stays at zero. Then the ten output neurons turn those reactions into ten scores, squeezed so that they add up to 100%.

The squeezing step has a name, softmax, and we meet it again in Session 5. The score for 3 is 96%, and no other digit gets more than 3%. This is the answer, plus how sure the network is.

title.text:
A person picks hand-made
features. A network finds its own.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t01_handlearned_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A person picks hand-made features. A network finds its own.

objects.text: Ask which one you can explain to a customer or a regulator.

runs.text: Hand-made: easy to explain, suits narrow, steady tasks.
Learned: needs many labelled examples.
Learned: hard to explain in one sentence.

slides.notes:
You have now seen both. The feature scatter earlier used two measurements chosen by a person, and one line separated the digits well. The neuron results used no chosen measurements: the network found its own, from the examples. Hand-made features are easy to explain and suit narrow, steady tasks, like checking a form layout.

Learned features cope with messier pictures but need many labelled examples and are harder to explain. For your own work, the question is which one you could defend to a customer, an auditor or a regulator if they asked why a decision was made.

title.text:
Training is the loop from Session 0: the
network is right more often each pass

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t01_learning_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Training is the loop from Session 0: the network is right more often each pass

objects.text: After 1 pass it is close to guessing. After 200 it reads most digits.

runs.text: Start: 17% right. Guessing among ten digits gives about 10%.
Each pass: guess, measure the error, adjust.
The same neuron looks different after training.

slides.notes:
This is your training loop from Session 0, drawn from a real run. Pass 1 means the network has looked at every training image once. It is right 17% of the time on images it has never seen. Pure guessing among ten digits would give about 10%. After 20 passes it is at 66%, after 50 at 92%, and after 200 at 97%.

Each pass is guess, measure the error, adjust, repeat. On the right, one neuron after 1 pass and the same neuron after 200 passes. The weights have moved. That movement is the learning.

title.text:
Demonstration: I train the digit
network and you watch it learn

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_7.30x3.90_ddcd0f6c.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: I train the digit network and you watch it learn

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: One image as plain numbers before any picture is drawn
The accuracy rising pass by pass
The mistakes, and which digits it confuses

slides.notes:
Now I run it for you. The script is called digits_run.py and it takes a few seconds on a laptop. First it loads the 1,797 handwritten digits that come with scikit-learn. It prints one image as 64 numbers. Then it trains the network with 1,347 images and holds back 450 that it never trains on.

Watch the accuracy on those 450 rise as the passes go up. Then we look at the mistakes. The same script produced every number on today’s slides, in a recorded run on 5 November 2026. If it fails on the day, I show the saved output.

title.text:
Recorded run: 8 right answers and
the first 4 mistakes on unseen digits

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t01_gallery_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Recorded run: 8 right answers and the first 4 mistakes on unseen digits

objects.text: Recorded run, 5 November 2026. Mistakes have red frames. 436 of 450 right.

slides.notes:
These are real test images, which means images the network never trained on. The top row and the first two on the second row are the first eight test images, and all eight are right. The four red frames are the first four of fourteen mistakes. Look at them as a person: that 8 really does look like a 1 at this size, and the 5 is hard even for us.

Some mistakes are understandable and some are not. Notice also that the network never says I do not know. It always gives a digit. Remember that when a system reads your scans.

title.text:
On digits it has never seen, the
network is right 436 times in 450

objects.text: of 450 unseen handwritten digits were read correctly.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_waffle_4.40x4.30_0f1522a0.png
objects.alt: On digits it has never seen, the network is right 436 times in 450

objects.text: Source: Recorded run, scikit-learn digits, 5 November 2026. Five random starts gave between 96% and 97%.

slides.notes:
So 436 of 450 is 97%. I ran the whole training five times with different random starting weights, and every run landed between 96% and 97%. That tells you the result is steady and not a lucky draw. It is good, but keep the setting in mind: these are tidy 8 by 8 digits, centred and cleaned, from a research dataset.

Real handwriting on a real form is harder. Session 3 gives you the proper way to measure a model, with precision, recall and thresholds. For now, one number on unseen data is the right place to start.

title.text:
Move the digit one pixel and
the same network falls to 46%

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t01_shift_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Move the digit one pixel and the same network falls to 46%

objects.text: It learned pixel patterns in fixed places.

runs.text: Training digits were centred. Shifted ones were never seen.
A person reads a shifted 3 at once.
A model is only as good as the cases it saw.

slides.notes:
Here is the honest limit. I took the same 450 test digits and slid each one a single pixel to the right. Accuracy fell from 97% to 46%. Two pixels, and it falls to 14%. A person would read all three pictures as a 3 without noticing the difference.

This small network learned patterns of dark pixels in fixed places. Networks built for pictures, called convolutional networks, are designed to cope with shifts much better, so do not conclude that all image systems are this fragile. Do conclude that you must test a system on the pictures it will really meet.

title.text:
Reading images appears in every function:
what goes in, what comes out, what you check

rows.text: Photo of stock in the depot

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.34.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_people_0.34.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shop_0.50.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shield_0.34.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_doc_0.50.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_tag_0.50.png

objects.text: These are uses of the same family of technique, with larger networks. Test each on your own images.

slides.notes:
Here is where this shows up in your own functions. In finance, a scanned invoice goes in and a supplier, date and total come out. In HR, a photo of a certificate. In operations, a photo of stock in the depot, and a count of bags comes back.

In compliance, a signature page, and the answer is signed or blank. In legal, a scanned court bundle becomes text, and names and figures can be misread. In sales, a photo of a shelf. These use bigger networks from the same family. The last column matters most: what would a person check, and how would you know the system works on your images?

title.text:
Score five payments with the risk
checklist, then change one weight

objects.text: 25 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Work through the one-page worksheet: five payments, three questions.

runs.text: Tick each question for each payment: 1 or 0.
Multiply by the weights 3, 2 and 1. Add. Flag at 4 or more.
Now give "amount over UGX 1,200,000" a weight of 4. Which payment changes?
Say whether you would accept that change, and why.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_3a92ad53.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: A scored worksheet and one sentence on the weights you would choose.

slides.notes:
This is the paper exercise, twenty-five minutes, no computer. Your worksheet has five payments. For each one, tick the three questions, multiply by the weights 3, 2 and 1, add them up, and flag anything at 4 or more. Then change one thing: the weight for a big amount goes from 3 to 4.

Which payment changes its answer?

Then decide whether you would accept that change and say why. There is no single right answer to the last part. You are doing exactly what training does automatically: adjusting a weight and watching the results move.

title.text:
Where would a system that reads
pictures help or hurt in your work?

objects.text: Pick one place in your job where pictures or scans are read by people today. What should happen?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.80.png

objects.text: Use it now
Low cost of a mistake, and a person can check quickly

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_people_0.80.png

objects.text: Use it with a checker
A person reviews every flagged case

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_clock_0.80.png

objects.text: Wait
Our images are poor or unusual: test first

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shield_0.80.png

objects.text: Do not use it
A mistake costs too much to catch
Write your decision and the reason in your workbook.

slides.notes:
Fifteen minutes on your own work. Think of one place in your job where a person reads pictures or scans today: invoices, identity documents, photos of goods, signed pages. Which of these four fits?

Use it now, if a mistake is cheap and a person can check quickly. Use it with a checker, if every flagged case is reviewed. Wait, if your images are poor or unusual and you need to test first. Do not use it, if a missed mistake costs too much.

Tell me your choice and the reason. The reason matters more than the choice.

title.text:
Keep the sheet: it is the
whole session on one page

objects.text: What you keep from today

runs.text: A one-page sheet: how a picture becomes numbers, the payment-risk neuron worked by hand, and the digit results.

objects.text: Our question today
How can a machine read a picture when all it has is numbers?
Next session
Session 2: Learning from examples: types of machine learning, decision trees, nearest neighbours.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_card_4.10x4.50_efd557b2.png

slides.notes:
Keep the one-page sheet. It has the payment-risk neuron worked by hand, the numbers from today’s run, and the one limit to remember: a network is good at what it has seen. If you use any system that reads images or scans in your work, ask what it was trained on and how it was checked.

We began with this question: How can a machine read a picture when all it has is numbers? Before you go, say in one sentence what you can now say about it.
